title: Same Book, Different Pages
principle: Which pages a cell reads is called gene expression.

t: A cell in your eye and a cell in your liver have exactly the same instructions. They are not remotely the same.
Every cell in your body carries an identical genome. A neuron and a liver cell share every letter of it and have almost nothing else in common.
sub: Same book. So what is different?
If the instructions are identical, the difference cannot be in the instructions.

question: If two cells have the same instructions, why are they different?
Given identical genomes, what accounts for the difference between cell types?
options: They read different parts of it
One of them has lost some instructions
They must have different instructions after all
stages.outcome: They read different parts of it
note: Commit. Two of these were seriously proposed, and one was disproved by cloning a frog.

stages.label: Which cell?
captions: A stem cell: hardly anything switched on yet.
A muscle cell: the muscle pages on, the rest shut.
A liver cell: a different set on, and it makes different things.
A nerve cell: different again — and all four have the same book.
t: Move through four different cells. Watch which pages are open.
Four cell types, one genome. Watch which genes are switched on in each.
after: Same book every time. Only the open pages change.
Nothing was added or removed. What changed is which genes are being read.

stages.label: Proportion of genes active
captions: Stem cell: broadly permissive chromatin, few lineage genes committed.
Muscle: myogenic programme on, alternative lineages actively repressed.
Liver: ~50% of genes expressed, but a different 50%.
Neuron: highest transcriptional diversity of any human cell type.
t: Work out what is actually varying between these cells, given the genome is constant.
The genome is invariant across all four. Identify what the varying quantity is, and note that repression is as active a process as activation.
after: Roughly half of all genes are on in any given cell — a different half each time.
Differentiation is not subtraction. Alternative programmes are actively repressed rather than absent, which is precisely why a differentiated nucleus can be reprogrammed at all.

t: Which pages a cell reads is called gene expression.
Which genes a cell is reading at any moment is its pattern of gene expression.
Gene expression: the regulated transcription of a subset of the genome. Identity is a expression state, not a genomic one.

Regulation is where the complexity lives. Human and chimpanzee protein-coding sequence differs by little more than one percent; most of what distinguishes them is when and where genes are switched on.
sub: Nothing gets thrown away. It just gets switched off.
The unused instructions are still there, intact — which is a testable claim, and it was tested.
Gurdon transplanted a nucleus from an intestinal cell into an egg and grew a whole frog, proving nothing had been discarded. Fifty years later the same logic gave induced pluripotent stem cells.
Gurdon in 1962 and Yamanaka in 2006 share the 2012 Nobel for the two halves of that argument: the differentiated nucleus retains everything, and four transcription factors are enough to send it back.

q: What is different between a liver cell and a nerve cell?
What differs between two cell types in the same body?
What is the locus of difference between differentiated cell types?
why: They both have all the instructions. They are just reading different bits — and the bits they are not reading are still there.
The genome is identical; the expression pattern is not. This is why a skin cell can be reprogrammed back into something that can become anything — nothing was ever thrown away.

Difference is regulatory, not genomic. The strongest evidence is reversibility: somatic cell nuclear transfer produces a whole organism from a differentiated nucleus, which would be impossible if differentiation involved loss.

t: Doctors can turn a bit of your skin back into a cell that could become anything.

Induced pluripotent stem cells are made by switching a handful of genes back on in an ordinary adult cell. They let researchers grow a patient's own neurons in a dish to test a drug on the actual disease, and they sidestep the ethical objections to embryonic sources entirely.
